questions.stem: What is the original source of the variation natural selection acts on?
options: Useful changes individuals develop in life and pass to their offspring
Deliberate genetic changes made by organisms when the habitat changes
Environmental pressure directly rewriting DNA so individuals fit better
Random mutations, with the reshuffling of genes in sexual reproduction
questions.explanation: Variation arises from random mutation and, in sexually reproducing species, from recombination and the mixing of parental alleles; the environment then selects among that pre-existing variation. The option about changes developed during an individual's lifetime is the classic Lamarckian misconception — a stretched neck or trained muscle is not encoded in gametes, so it is not inherited. The cue: selection edits variation that is already present, it does not create it to order.

questions.stem: Comparing DNA sequences of a gene found in humans, chimpanzees, mice and yeast supports the idea that all organisms are related to some degree. Which result would be expected?
options: Yeast is most similar to humans, because simpler organisms change more slowly than complex ones
All four share recognisably similar sequences, with human and chimpanzee most alike and yeast least alike
Only human and chimpanzee share the gene, since yeast and mice are too distantly related to have it
All four have identical sequences, because a gene doing the same job cannot change over time
questions.explanation: Genes inherited from a distant common ancestor persist across very different lineages, and the number of accumulated sequence differences grows with time since the lineages split — so degree of similarity tracks closeness of relatedness. The option that only humans and chimps have the gene misses the central claim of the description, that relatedness extends to all organisms including yeast. Identical sequences are not expected, because neutral changes accumulate even in conserved genes.

questions.stem: A mountain range splits one lizard population in two, and they become separate species. What was its role?
options: It caused geographic isolation, so the two gene pools could no longer mix
It caused mutations in the lizards, creating the differences between groups
It removed all variation from each group, so each became identical
It forced the lizards to adapt deliberately to conditions on each side
questions.explanation: Isolation stops gene flow, so mutations and different selection pressures on each side accumulate independently until the groups can no longer interbreed. The option saying the range caused mutations is tempting because change did follow the barrier, but mutations occur randomly regardless of barriers — the barrier only stops the mixing. The cue: barriers block gene flow; they do not generate variation or make organisms choose to change.

questions.stem: Vertebrate embryos of fish, chickens and humans all show pharyngeal (gill) arches early in development, even though only fish develop gills. What does comparative embryology conclude from this?
options: These groups inherited a shared developmental pattern from a common ancestor
Human embryos briefly pass through the adult fish stage of their ancestry
Each group evolved gill arches separately because embryos live in fluid
Gill arches prove that fish are the direct ancestors of humans and chickens
questions.explanation: Shared early developmental structures are best explained by descent from a common ancestor whose developmental program has been retained and later modified in each lineage. The option about passing through an adult fish stage is the discredited idea that embryos replay adult ancestral forms — the arches resemble embryonic structures, not adult fish. The cue: embryology shows shared ancestry and shared development, not a replay of adult ancestors or a direct ancestor–descendant line between living groups.

questions.stem: A population of insects is sprayed with a new insecticide. Almost all die, but a few survive and their descendants rebuild the population, which is now hard to kill with that spray. What is the best explanation?
options: The whole population gradually built up a tolerance by being exposed repeatedly
A few insects already carried alleles conferring resistance, and the spray selected for them
The spray caused the surviving insects to become resistant during their lifetime
The insects that needed resistance most developed it and passed it to their young
questions.explanation: Resistance alleles arise by random mutation before the spray is used; the insecticide is the selection pressure that kills susceptible insects and leaves resistant ones to breed, raising the frequency of resistance. The option saying the spray caused resistance in survivors reverses cause and effect — the chemical does not induce the useful change, it just filters. The cue: ask whether the trait existed before the pressure appeared; in natural selection it always did.

questions.stem: Dolphins and sharks both have streamlined bodies and fins, but dolphins are more closely related to cows than to sharks. What does this show about using body shape as evidence of relatedness?
options: Dolphins and sharks must share a recent aquatic ancestor that cows also descend from
Living in the same habitat causes species to gradually become the same species
Similar selection pressures can produce similar shapes in distantly related lineages
Body shape is always the most reliable indicator of how closely species are related
questions.explanation: Convergent evolution means unrelated lineages facing the same physical demands, such as fast swimming, can evolve similar external forms, so overall shape can mislead; internal structure, embryology and DNA give better evidence of ancestry. The option claiming a recent shared aquatic ancestor is tempting because the animals look alike, but dolphin skeletons, lungs and embryos group them firmly with mammals. The cue: shared ancestry is judged by deep structural and genetic similarity, not surface resemblance.

questions.stem: What do biologists mean by 'variation' within a population?
options: Individuals of one species differ in inherited features such as size or colour
Individuals of one species change during life in response to their environment
Different species in one habitat differ in the features that suit them to it
Individuals are born identical but differ through the food and shelter they get
questions.explanation: Variation refers to the inherited differences that exist between individuals of the same species, and it is this heritable variation that natural selection acts on. The option about individuals changing during their lifetime describes acquired characteristics, which are not passed to offspring and so cannot drive evolution. Differences between separate species are not variation within a population. Cue: variation is within one species, present at birth, and inheritable.

questions.stem: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria spreads far faster than most evolutionary change in animals. Which combination of factors best accounts for this?
options: Bacteria are able to sense antibiotics and deliberately alter their DNA to build the resistance genes they need to survive
Antibiotics act as a mutagen that reliably converts ordinary bacteria into resistant bacteria within a single generation
Bacteria have far more DNA than animals, so each individual bacterium carries more useful variation to be selected from
Very short generation times and huge population sizes, combined with strong selection that kills nearly all non-resistant bacteria
questions.explanation: Evolution is faster when many generations pass quickly, when populations are large enough to contain rare beneficial variants, and when the selection pressure is intense. The option about bacteria deliberately altering their DNA wrongly treats mutation as goal-directed — mutations arise randomly and the antibiotic only selects among what is already present. Bacteria actually have much smaller genomes than animals. Cue: rate of evolution depends on generation time, population size and strength of selection.

questions.stem: Whale flippers, bat wings and human arms all contain one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones and digits, despite doing very different jobs. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: These limbs are homologous, inherited from a shared ancestor with that bone pattern and modified for different functions
These limbs are analogous, having evolved the same internal bone pattern separately because each function demands it
The pattern shows whales, bats and humans all evolved directly from one another in a single straight line of descent
The pattern is coincidence, since bone arrangement is not inherited and is determined by how a limb is used in life
questions.explanation: A shared underlying structure used for different functions is the signature of homology — common ancestry followed by modification through natural selection. Calling them analogous is the tempting error: analogous structures share a FUNCTION but differ in underlying structure, such as insect and bird wings, which is the opposite pattern here. Descent is also branching, not a straight line from one modern species to another. Cue: same structure, different function means homologous.

questions.stem: What does biogeography actually study?
options: Where living and extinct species are found, and how barriers shaped that
The seasonal migration routes animals take between feeding and breeding
The embryo stages shared by vertebrate groups before birth or hatching
The chemical dating of rock layers to age the fossils they contain
questions.explanation: Biogeography examines where species live and lived, and links those patterns to the movement and separation of landmasses — Australia's distinctive marsupials, for example, reflect long isolation of the continent. Migration routes sound geographic, but tracking where individuals travel each year says nothing about how species arose in particular places. The cue is 'bio' plus 'geography': species distribution over long timescales, not individual journeys.

questions.stem: During a long drought on an island, only large, hard seeds remain. Over several years the average beak depth of the finch population increases. Which explanation fits natural selection?
options: The drought caused mutations in the finches that produced deeper beaks, because deeper beaks were what the birds needed
The finches sensed that seeds had hardened and their bodies responded by producing offspring with the required beak shape
Finches that already had deeper beaks survived and bred more, so beak-depth alleles they carried became more common
Individual finches strengthened and deepened their beaks by cracking hard seeds, and their chicks hatched with those beaks
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on variation that already exists: the population contained a range of beak depths, and in drought conditions the deeper-beaked birds fed better, survived and left more offspring, shifting the population average. The idea that beaks strengthened through use and were then inherited is tempting because the birds really are cracking hard seeds, but wear and use do not alter the alleles in gametes. The cue is that selection sorts pre-existing variation rather than creating what is needed.

questions.stem: Birds on a remote volcanic island resemble species on the nearest mainland 600 km away far more than they resemble birds on a distant island with an almost identical climate. What does this pattern best support?
options: The island birds descended from mainland colonists and diverged after isolation, rather than being formed to suit the climate
Identical climates always produce identical species, so the two islands must differ in climate more than measurements show
Species are distributed randomly across the globe, so any resemblance between island and mainland birds is coincidence
Island species migrate regularly to the mainland to interbreed, which keeps the two groups looking similar to each other
questions.explanation: Biogeography repeatedly shows that a region's species resemble their geographic neighbours rather than organisms in similar habitats elsewhere, which is what you expect if populations colonise nearby land and then diverge in isolation. The 'identical climates always produce identical species' option is tempting because climate does influence adaptation, but similar climates on separated landmasses regularly hold quite unrelated organisms. The cue is that ancestry and geographic proximity, not habitat matching, explain the pattern.

questions.stem: A single population of beetles is split by a widening river. Thousands of years later the halves cannot interbreed. Which combination of processes best accounts for this speciation?
options: Loss of all variation in each group, since small separated populations end up genetically identical within themselves
Inherited variation in each group, isolation preventing gene flow, and different selection pressures on either side of the river
Isolation alone, because any two separated populations must eventually become different species given enough time
Identical selection pressures on both sides, which drive the two groups apart because separated groups cannot stay alike
questions.explanation: Speciation needs raw material (heritable variation), a barrier to gene flow (isolation) so differences are not blended away, and selection or drift pushing the groups along different paths until they are reproductively incompatible. 'Isolation alone' is the most tempting error because isolation is essential, but two isolated groups in near-identical conditions with little genetic change can remain able to interbreed. The cue is that isolation permits divergence; it does not by itself cause it.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions must all be present for natural selection to change a population over generations?
options: Heritable variation, complete isolation by a physical barrier, and a mutation arising in direct response to the new conditions
Variation between individuals, that variation being heritable, and differences in survival or reproduction linked to that variation
Identical individuals, a sudden environmental change, and a long period of geographic isolation from other populations
Variation between individuals, a conscious effort by organisms to improve, and a rapid increase in population size
questions.explanation: Natural selection needs raw variation, that variation must be passed on genetically, and it must make a difference to how many offspring individuals leave — those three together shift trait frequencies. The option including isolation and a mutation arising in response is tempting because isolation matters for speciation, but selection itself does not require a barrier, and mutations arise randomly rather than in response to need. Cue: isolation splits populations; selection changes them.

questions.stem: Comparative embryology, homologous bones and DNA comparisons all point to the same conclusion about relatedness. What does the theory of evolution say relatedness between any two living species means?
options: Relatedness means the species live in the same region and have been shaped by the same environment
They share a common ancestor at some point in the past; closer relatives share a more recent common ancestor
The more closely related species evolved from the less closely related one that is alive today
Relatedness means the species are at similar stages on a single ladder of progress from simple to complex
questions.explanation: Evolution describes a branching pattern: every pair of species traces back to a shared ancestral population, and 'more closely related' simply means that shared ancestor is more recent. The idea that one living species evolved from another is a common error — humans and chimpanzees, for example, share an ancestor that was neither. Cue: relatedness is about branching points in the past, not a ranking of living things or shared habitat.

questions.stem: What does the fossil record contribute as evidence for evolution?
options: It shows life forms changing through successive rock layers over long spans
It provides a complete record of every species that has ever lived
It shows all major groups appearing together in the deepest rock layers
It records the DNA of extinct organisms so ancestors can be identified
questions.explanation: Fossils are preserved in sedimentary layers, with deeper layers generally older, so the record shows how the types of organisms present have changed over enormous time spans. The claim that it is a complete record is false: fossilisation is rare and requires particular conditions, so the record has many gaps. The idea that all groups appear together in the deepest layers contradicts the observed order, in which groups such as fish appear well before mammals. Remember the fossil record is a sequence, not a full catalogue.

questions.stem: In evolutionary biology, what is an adaptation?
options: A feature that appears only after an environment has already stopped changing
A heritable feature that improves survival or reproduction in a particular environment
A change an individual makes during its lifetime to cope with its surroundings
A deliberate change a population produces because it needs a new feature
questions.explanation: An adaptation is an inherited characteristic that has become common in a population because it gave individuals better survival or reproductive success in their environment. The option about an individual changing during its lifetime describes acclimatisation, such as getting fitter or tanning, which is not passed to offspring and so is not an adaptation in the evolutionary sense. Adaptations also cannot be produced on demand, since variation arises before selection acts. The cue is the word heritable.

questions.stem: Which observation is evidence from comparative embryology rather than fossils or biogeography?
options: Embryos of turtles, chickens and pigs pass through similar early stages
Extinct horses with fewer toes appear in progressively younger rock layers
Islands near a mainland share more species with it than with far islands
Bacteria in a hospital ward become antibiotic-resistant within a few years
questions.explanation: Comparative embryology compares the developmental stages of different species, and shared early stages point to shared ancestry. The horse toe sequence in rock layers is fossil evidence, and the island species pattern is biogeography, so both are real evidence for evolution but from other lines. The antibiotic example is directly observed selection in action, not embryology. Match the evidence to what is actually being compared: embryos, rocks, distributions or living populations.

questions.stem: Human wisdom teeth and the tiny hip bones inside whales are described as vestigial structures. What do vestigial structures suggest about evolution?
options: They show that some organisms evolved without any ancestors of their own
They prove that an organism's structures never change once a species exists
They are reduced remnants of features that were functional in an ancestral species
They are new features that are still forming and will be fully functional in future
questions.explanation: A vestigial structure is a reduced, largely non-functional remnant of a structure that was useful to an ancestor, such as the pelvic bones inherited from land-living whale ancestors. Calling them features that are still forming reverses the direction of change; selection does not build toward a future need, and the fossil record shows these structures were larger in ancestors. The cue is that vestigial means left over, not under construction.

questions.stem: A racehorse builds muscle by training and carries a gene for long leg bones. Which passes to its foals?
options: Both, since anything a parent gains in life is copied to offspring
Neither, since evolution only involves brand new mutations in the foal
The gene for long leg bones only, since only changes in DNA are inherited
The trained muscles only, since they were built in the foal's environment
questions.explanation: Evolution by natural selection requires heritable variation, and only differences carried in DNA are passed through gametes to offspring. The tempting choice is that both traits are inherited, but muscle built by training is an acquired characteristic that alters body tissue, not the parent's genetic information. The option saying neither is inherited is also false: existing gene variants are inherited every generation, not just newly arisen mutations. Cue: ask whether the change is in the DNA passed on, or only in the body during life.

questions.stem: Australia has many native marsupials such as kangaroos, wombats and quolls, but very few native placental land mammals. How does biogeography explain this?
options: Placental mammals evolved into marsupials after arriving in Australia, which is why the two groups look alike
Australia separated from other landmasses long ago, so its mammals evolved in isolation from placental mammals elsewhere
Australia's climate is uniquely suited to marsupials, so marsupials evolved separately here and on every other dry continent
Marsupials are a more recently evolved group than placental mammals and have not yet spread beyond Australia
questions.explanation: Biogeography explains distributions by history: continental separation isolated Australian mammal lineages, so they diversified without competition from most placental groups. The climate option is false because dry climates elsewhere, such as in Africa and South America, are dominated by placental mammals, not independently evolved marsupials. Marsupials are not a newer group than placentals, and one modern group does not turn into another on arrival. Cue: biogeography asks where organisms are and how geography and history put them there.

questions.stem: In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock, fossils of jawless fish appear in the deepest layers, amphibians higher up, and mammals only in the upper layers. What does this pattern support?
options: Rock layers form in random order, so the position of fossils tells us nothing about their age
Major groups appeared in a time order consistent with branching from earlier ancestors
All major animal groups appeared at the same time and were later sorted by rock density
Mammals are the oldest vertebrate group, but their fossils were pushed upward by later movement
questions.explanation: In undisturbed sedimentary rock the deeper layers are older, so the order in which groups first appear is a record of the order in which they arose, matching the branching pattern evolution predicts. The suggestion that fossils were sorted by density is false: fossils are entombed where the sediment was laid down, they do not float or sink through solid rock. Mammals are not the oldest vertebrate group, and undisturbed layers are laid down oldest first, not randomly. Cue: deeper equals older unless the rock has clearly been folded or overturned.

questions.stem: A biologist calls two frog populations 'isolated'. What does that mean?
options: Frogs within each population avoid one another, so each breeds without a partner
The two populations now live in identical habitats and face the same pressures
Each population has lost all variation, so every individual is identical
Gene flow between them has stopped, so they no longer interbreed
questions.explanation: Isolation in evolution means a barrier (often geographic) prevents breeding between two groups, so alleles arising in one group cannot spread to the other and the groups can diverge. The option about identical habitats reverses the point: isolation matters because the separated groups usually face different pressures and drift apart, not because conditions become the same. Cue: isolation is about the flow of genes between populations being blocked, not about individuals or variation disappearing.

questions.stem: A beetle species living on pale sand includes both pale and dark individuals. Some beetles colonise a nearby field of dark volcanic rock, where birds hunt them by sight. After many generations almost all beetles on the rock are dark. What is the best explanation?
options: The beetles needed to be dark to survive, so mutations for dark colour were produced in response
Pale beetles changed their colour to dark during their lifetimes to avoid being eaten by the birds
Dark beetles were less often spotted and eaten, so they left more offspring and dark variants became common
The dark rock surface caused the beetles' bodies to darken, and their darkened bodies were passed on
questions.explanation: The variation in colour already existed; predation acted as the selection pressure, so the better-camouflaged variant survived and reproduced more, raising its frequency each generation. The option saying mutations were produced in response to need is a common trap: mutations occur randomly and are not made to order by the environment, which only decides which existing variants do better. Cue: selection filters variation that is already present.

questions.stem: Fossils of early marsupials are found in South America, Antarctica and Australia, and living marsupials are concentrated in Australia and South America. Which conclusion do biogeography and the fossil record best support together?
options: Marsupials spread across landmasses that were once joined, then diverged after the continents separated
Marsupials evolved separately on each continent because each continent had a similar climate
Marsupials must have swum thousands of kilometres of open ocean between the modern continents
Marsupials arose in Australia only, and all fossils found elsewhere are of unrelated placental mammals
questions.explanation: Biogeography combines the geographic distribution of living and fossil species with what geology says about moving continents: a shared ancestral population on connected land, later split by separation, explains both the fossil trail and the modern distribution. The independent-evolution-in-similar-climates option is tempting because similar climates can produce similar body forms, but it cannot explain the shared fossil lineage across the three landmasses. Cue: biogeography asks where relatives are found and why, using Earth's history as part of the explanation.

questions.stem: The fossil record supports evolution, yet scientists still expect it to be incomplete. Which statement best explains why gaps exist?
options: Fossilisation needs uncommon conditions such as rapid burial, and many fossils are later eroded or never found
Soft-bodied organisms decayed rather than fossilising, which shows those groups never actually existed
Rocks and fossils older than a few million years cannot be dated, so older layers are left blank
Every organism that lived left a fossil, but almost all of those fossils formed in a single rock layer
questions.explanation: Preservation is rare: it usually needs hard parts plus quick burial in sediment, and even preserved fossils can be destroyed by erosion, metamorphism or simply remain undiscovered. The option about soft-bodied organisms is tempting because soft tissue really does fossilise poorly, but concluding those groups never existed is false — poor preservation is about the record, not about the organisms. Cue: gaps are a limitation of how fossils form and are found, not evidence against evolution.

questions.stem: Which of these features of an organism could be inherited by its offspring and so contribute to evolution by natural selection?
options: A difference in fur colour caused by a variant of a pigment gene
A scar on the leg from an injury during a fight
Extra body fat gained from a season of plentiful food
A missing tail tip lost to frostbite during a cold winter
questions.explanation: Only variation carried in the genes (in the DNA passed on through gametes) can be inherited, so only genetic differences such as a pigment gene variant can accumulate under selection. Extra body fat from plentiful food is tempting because it clearly affects survival, but it is acquired during the animal's life and is not written into its DNA, so it is not passed to offspring. The cue: ask whether the trait came from the animal's genes or from something that happened to its body.

questions.stem: Which finding would be classed as evidence for evolution from the fossil record?
options: Mice and humans sharing very similar sequences of a blood protein gene
A series of dated fossils showing horse-like animals with progressively fewer toes
Chicken and human embryos both showing a tail-like structure early in development
Flightless birds occurring on several southern continents but not in Europe
questions.explanation: The fossil record is evidence drawn from preserved remains in dated rock layers, so a dated series showing gradual change in toe number fits it exactly. Embryos sharing tail-like structures is tempting evidence for relatedness, but it comes from comparative embryology, not from fossils. Check what is actually being examined: rocks and remains, developing embryos, geographic distribution, or molecules.

questions.stem: Two islands off the same coast have almost identical climates, but the finches on each island have differently shaped beaks. Which statement about this is consistent with natural selection?
options: The islands' finches must be unrelated species that never shared an ancestor
Different food sources on each island favoured different beak shapes in each population
The finches changed their beak shapes to match the seeds they preferred to eat
Beaks differ because climate is the only factor that can drive natural selection
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on whatever variation exists when a specific selection pressure differs — here, differences in available food, not climate, can favour different beak shapes on each island. The idea that the finches 'changed their beak shapes to match' the seeds reverses the logic: variation in beak shape already existed, and the food supply determined which variants survived and bred best. Watch for wording that gives organisms the power to change themselves.

questions.stem: Two populations of snails on the same hillside are separated by a wide, permanent strip of bare rock they cannot cross. Which statement best describes the effect of this isolation on their evolution?
options: It prevents mutation from occurring in either population, freezing both as they are
It guarantees both populations will evolve identical adaptations because conditions match
Gene flow between them stops, so differences can build up independently in each population
It immediately creates two new species, because separation itself defines a species
questions.explanation: Isolation matters because it halts gene flow — the two groups no longer share genetic variation, so mutations and selection accumulate separately in each. Saying separation immediately creates two species is the most common slip: speciation takes many generations of divergence until the populations can no longer interbreed successfully. Remember isolation is the starting condition for divergence, not the finish line.

questions.stem: A student says, 'Bacteria became resistant because the antibiotic caused them to develop resistance genes.' Which correction best fits the theory of evolution by natural selection?
options: Bacteria detected the antibiotic and switched on new genes they built for the purpose
Resistance appeared because the bacteria that most needed it reproduced more often
Resistance variants already existed by chance; the antibiotic only selected which cells survived
The antibiotic weakened all cells equally, and the survivors then strengthened over time
questions.explanation: Mutations arise randomly and independently of need, so resistance variants are present in the population before the antibiotic is used; the drug then acts as the selection pressure that kills susceptible cells. The claim that bacteria detect the antibiotic and build genes for the purpose is appealing but reverses cause and effect — the environment selects existing variation, it does not order up new genes. The cue phrase to distrust is any option where the organism responds to a need by producing the trait.

questions.stem: Vertebrate limb bones, DNA sequences and early embryo structures all point to relatedness. What does the theory of evolution claim about relatedness between any two living species?
options: Species are related only if they can still interbreed and produce fertile offspring
Relatedness exists only among animals, since plants and microbes have separate origins
Both descend from a common ancestor, differing only in how long ago that ancestor lived
Only species in the same class descend from a common ancestor; other groups arose separately
questions.explanation: Evolution treats the tree of life as continuous: every pair of species shares an ancestor somewhere, and closer relatives simply share a more recent one. Restricting relatedness to species that can interbreed confuses relatedness with belonging to the same species — cows and whales cannot interbreed yet clearly share ancestry. Think of relatedness as a matter of how far back the shared ancestor is, not as a yes-or-no boundary.

questions.stem: Cacti in the Americas and unrelated euphorbia plants in Africa both have thick water-storing stems and spines instead of leaves. What do biogeography and evolutionary theory conclude from this pattern?
options: The two groups must be closely related, since such detailed similarity cannot arise twice
Cactus seeds must have drifted to Africa, so the African plants are the same species
Spines and thick stems appeared because the plants shared the same recent ancestor
Similar dry-climate selection pressures produced similar adaptations in two separate lineages
questions.explanation: When lineages on different continents face the same conditions, selection can favour similar adaptations independently, which is why appearance alone is unreliable for judging relatedness. The claim that such detailed similarity cannot arise twice is tempting, but it ignores that a shared environmental pressure acting on separate lineages routinely produces look-alike solutions. Distribution across continents plus separate ancestry is the signature of independent adaptation, not close kinship.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes what natural selection changes over time?
options: Each individual gradually alters its own inherited traits to suit its surroundings
Every individual in the population acquires the useful trait during its lifetime
The environment directly rewrites the DNA of individuals to supply needed traits
The proportions of inherited variants in a population shift across generations
questions.explanation: Natural selection works because individuals differ in inherited traits and some leave more offspring, so the make-up of the population changes across generations — populations evolve, individuals do not. The option about each individual altering its own inherited traits is the common Lamarckian error: an animal's traits can change during life (through growth, use or injury), but such changes are not passed on. The cue is to ask what is inherited and what is counted over a whole population.

questions.stem: Fossils show animals with reptile teeth and feathers, dated between reptiles and birds. What do they support?
options: Modern birds evolved directly from the reptile species alive today
A full set of bird features appeared in one generation from reptile parents
Each fossil species is an isolated form unrelated to any living group
Major groups share common ancestors, with features accumulating gradually
questions.explanation: Transitional fossils show intermediate combinations of features in the expected time order, which is what descent with modification from shared ancestors predicts. Saying birds evolved from today's reptiles is wrong because living reptiles are cousins, not ancestors — both lines descend from extinct ancestral species. The cue is that ancestors are always extinct populations, never modern species.

questions.stem: The fossil record, biogeography, comparative embryology and DNA comparisons all produce broadly the same pattern of relatedness among living groups. Why does this agreement strengthen the theory of evolution?
options: It shows that evolutionary change must happen quickly enough to be seen in every kind of evidence
Independent methods reaching the same pattern makes it unlikely the pattern is an error of any one method
It converts the theory into a proven fact that scientists can no longer revise with new data
Each line of evidence is not scientific on its own and only becomes valid when combined with others
questions.explanation: Scientific confidence grows when separate, independent kinds of evidence converge, because the flaws or biases of one method would not be expected to produce the same result in the others. The 'proven fact, no longer revisable' option is tempting because the evidence is very strong, but scientific theories always remain open to testing and refinement. The cue is that convergence increases confidence, it does not close inquiry.

questions.stem: Cheetahs have unusually low genetic variation compared with most large mammals. What does evolutionary theory predict about this population if a new disease appears?
options: The population will survive because individuals exposed to the disease will build resistance and pass it to cubs
The population is at greater risk, because there is little inherited variation for selection to act on
The population will quickly evolve resistance, because low variation lets a helpful mutation spread faster
The population is unaffected, because resistance genes appear in response to whichever disease arrives
questions.explanation: Natural selection can only favour variants that already exist in the population, so low genetic variation means it is less likely that any individuals carry alleles giving resistance, leaving the whole population vulnerable. The option about a helpful mutation spreading faster misuses the idea: low variation does not speed up the appearance of new mutations, and it reduces the raw material selection needs. Remember that variation is the starting condition for selection, not something the threat itself supplies.

questions.stem: What supplies the differences between individuals that natural selection acts on?
options: Individuals gradually changing their bodies to suit the habitat
The environment altering genes so useful traits appear when needed
Parents passing on skills and features gained during their lifetime
Mutation and the reshuffling of genes during sexual reproduction
questions.explanation: Heritable variation arises from random mutation and from the new gene combinations produced during sexual reproduction; selection then acts on whatever variation already exists. The option about individuals gradually changing their bodies to suit the habitat is the classic Lamarckian error — an individual's body changes during life are not written back into its genes. The cue: selection can only pick from variation that is already present and inheritable, it cannot order variation to appear.

questions.stem: What does 'natural selection' describe?
options: Individuals with helpful traits surviving and reproducing more
Animals choosing to change their own bodies to suit the habitat
The strongest individual in every species always surviving
Species being deliberately bred by humans for useful traits
questions.explanation: Natural selection works because some inherited variations help an individual survive and breed, so those variations become more common. The tempting answer is that animals change themselves — they cannot; the variation is already there before the environment does the selecting.
questions.teaching:
Start from a fact about any population: its members are not identical. Some are faster, some better camouflaged, some more resistant to a particular disease — and a good deal of that difference is inherited rather than learned.

Now add an environment with no room for everyone. Whatever differences happen to be useful in that particular place get carried by a slightly larger share of the following generation, simply because their owners lived long enough to breed. Repeat across thousands of generations and the whole population shifts. Nothing is choosing or trying here. Animals do not alter their own bodies to suit conditions, and the environment has no plan — the differences are already present before it does anything with them.

questions.stem: Where does the variation natural selection acts on come from?
options: The food an animal chooses to eat
The climate an animal is born into
Random mutations and the mixing of genes
Habits an animal builds during its lifetime
questions.explanation: Variation arises from mutation and from genes being shuffled during reproduction. Habits acquired in a lifetime are the classic wrong answer: a trait has to be in the DNA to be passed on.
questions.teaching:
Selection can only work with differences that already exist, so the real question is where those differences originate — and whatever supplies them has to be heritable, or evolution can do nothing with it.

Two processes supply it. Copying DNA occasionally goes wrong, throwing up versions of a gene that nobody in the population had before. And every time sex cells form, the chromosomes inherited from two parents are shuffled and recombined, so siblings end up with different combinations from the same pair of parents. Neither process is aiming at anything useful. A skill you learn, a muscle you build or a habit you form is not written back into your DNA, so it stops with you.

questions.stem: What is a fossil?
options: A mineral that formed deep inside an active volcano
Preserved remains or traces of a once-living thing
Any rock found buried deep underground in layers
A bone from an animal that died recently
questions.explanation: A fossil is the preserved remains or trace — a bone, a shell, a footprint — of something that lived long ago. Not every buried rock qualifies, which is the usual over-generalisation.
questions.teaching:
Fossilisation is rare. Most organisms decay completely, so the fossil record is a thin and patchy sample rather than a full catalogue — usually only hard parts, and usually only where the remains were buried quickly in sediment.

Two kinds turn up. Some are the organism itself, or the minerals that gradually replaced it: bones, shells, teeth, wood. Others are marks the organism left behind while alive — footprints, burrows, droppings — which record behaviour rather than anatomy. Both count. What does not count is any old buried rock: age and depth alone do not make something one of these, and the link to a living thing is the whole point.

questions.stem: What is a species?
options: Any group of animals that live in the same habitat
A group of animals that look roughly alike from the outside
All the animals descended from one single individual
A group whose members can breed and produce fertile young
questions.explanation: The test is fertile offspring: members of a species can breed and their young can breed in turn. Looking alike is tempting but unreliable — a horse and a donkey produce a mule, which is infertile, so they are separate species.
questions.teaching:
"Looks similar" turns out to be a poor definition, because it fails in both directions. Great Danes and chihuahuas look nothing alike and are one species; some butterflies are indistinguishable and are several.

Biologists use a breeding test instead. The key detail is the word "fertile": a horse and a donkey can produce a mule, and the mule is healthy, but it cannot itself have offspring. So horses and donkeys stay separate. That fertility requirement is what the whole definition turns on, and it is what makes speciation identifiable — once two populations can no longer produce fertile young together, the split is complete.

questions.stem: What does extinction mean?
options: A species has become rare in one area
A species has split into two new ones
No living members of a species remain
A species has moved to a new habitat
questions.explanation: Extinction is final: the last individual has died and the species is gone. Becoming rare is the tempting answer, but a rare species still has living members and can recover.
questions.teaching:
It is worth being exact, because everyday speech uses the word loosely for anything rare or declining.

The condition it actually describes is final: not one individual survives anywhere on Earth, and nothing can bring the species back. That is different from being endangered, where numbers are low but a population still exists and can recover — humpback whales were down to a few thousand and are now over 100,000. It is also different from local disappearance, where a species is gone from one area but survives elsewhere. Around 99% of species that have ever lived have reached the final state described here.

questions.stem: What does DNA carry?
options: The instructions for an organism's inherited traits
The energy an organism needs in order to move and grow
A record of the food an organism has eaten
A record of the injuries an organism has suffered
questions.explanation: DNA stores the coded instructions that build and run an organism, and those are what pass to offspring. Confusing it with energy is common, but energy comes from food and is handled by other molecules entirely.
questions.teaching:
Cells run on several different kinds of molecule and each has its own job, so it helps to sort them.

Carbohydrates and fats store and supply energy. Proteins do most of the work — enzymes, muscle fibres, antibodies. And one molecule does none of that: it stores coded information. That code specifies which proteins the cell can build, and because a copy of it goes into every gamete, it is the route by which characteristics reach the next generation. It records nothing about what happened to the organism during its life — not what it ate, not what injuries it took. Only the code is passed on.

questions.stem: What is selective breeding?
options: Humans choosing which individuals reproduce
Animals choosing their own mates in the wild
A species adapting slowly without any help
Two different species breeding together
questions.explanation: In selective breeding people pick the parents, which is how we got wheat, sheepdogs and dairy cattle. Natural selection is the tempting answer, but there the environment does the choosing, not a person.
questions.teaching:
Every dog breed, every wheat variety and every dairy cow exists because people repeatedly chose which individuals were allowed to reproduce, generation after generation.

The mechanism is the same as in nature — inherited variation, differential reproduction, change over time — with one difference: who does the choosing. In the wild, the environment does it, and no intention is involved. Here a person picks the parents with an outcome in mind, so the process is far faster and can push traits well past anything that would survive unaided. Note it is not genetic engineering: nothing is edited directly, only the choice of parents.

questions.stem: Which of these is evidence for evolution?
options: Fossils showing gradual change over time
Animals in a zoo living longer than wild ones
The number of species alive today
Two animals sharing the same habitat
questions.explanation: Fossils in successive rock layers show forms changing across long spans of time, which is direct evidence. Sharing a habitat is tempting but says nothing about ancestry — unrelated species share habitats constantly.
questions.teaching:
Evidence for evolution has to show change over time, or shared ancestry, and several independent lines do.

The clearest is the layering of rock. Deeper layers are older, and the forms found in them differ systematically from those above, with intermediate forms appearing at the points you would expect. Other lines back it up: DNA comparisons that group species the same way anatomy does, limb bones with the same underlying arrangement in a bat's wing and a whale's flipper, and resistance evolving in bacteria within a laboratory. What is not evidence is a fact about the present with no time dimension — how many species exist now, or which share a habitat.

questions.stem: What is an adaptation?
options: A change made deliberately by an animal
A disease that spreads through a population
A feature that helps survival in a habitat
A habit learned during an animal's life
questions.explanation: An adaptation is an inherited feature that improves survival or breeding in a particular environment. Something learned in a lifetime is not inherited, so it cannot be an adaptation in this sense.
questions.teaching:
It is easy to read the word as though the animal did something deliberate — "the fox adapted to the cold". Individuals do not work that way. A fox cannot decide to grow thicker fur and then pass that decision on.

What the word actually names is an inherited characteristic that happens to suit the place an organism lives, and which has become common because ancestors carrying it left more descendants than those without it. So it is the product of many generations of selection rather than of one lifetime. The test is whether it is written into the DNA: something acquired during a single life, however useful it was to that individual, does not qualify.

questions.stem: How long ago did life first appear on Earth?
options: About 3.5 billion years
About 10 million years
About 65 million years
About 200 thousand years
questions.explanation: The earliest evidence of life is around 3.5 billion years old. 65 million years ago is the extinction of the non-bird dinosaurs, and 200 thousand is roughly when modern humans appear.
questions.teaching:
Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old, and life turns up surprisingly early in that story — within roughly the first billion years, as soon as conditions allowed.

The scale is the hard part. For most of that history life was single-celled; complex animals are a late arrival. If the whole of Earth's history were one day, the dinosaurs would appear in the last hour and humans in the final couple of seconds. Two other numbers often get confused with this one: 65 million years ago the non-bird dinosaurs died out, and modern humans appear around 200,000 years ago. Both are recent by comparison.

questions.stem: What is a common ancestor?
options: A species two groups both descend from
A species that still lives today
The oldest fossil ever found
A species with no living relatives
questions.explanation: A common ancestor is the species from which two later groups both descend. It is usually extinct, so looking for it among living species is the wrong place to search.
questions.teaching:
Evolution produces a branching tree rather than a ladder. Humans did not descend from chimpanzees; both descend from something else that is no longer around.

That branching point is what this term names — the population living at the fork, from which two later groups both trace back. Because it lived at the fork, it is almost always extinct, so looking for it among species alive today is the wrong search. The closer two species sit on the tree, the more recent their shared branching point and the more DNA they have in common, which is how genetic comparisons are used to work out how the tree is shaped.

questions.stem: What does the fossil record show about species?
options: They have changed over long periods
They have stayed the same throughout
They all appeared at the same time
They never leave any physical traces
questions.explanation: Successive rock layers hold different forms, showing change across time. The record is incomplete because fossilisation is rare, but the pattern of change through the layers is clear.
questions.teaching:
Because deeper rock layers are older, the fossils in them can be read in sequence, and the sequence is the whole point.

What it shows is that the forms present change as you move up through the layers. Species appear, persist, alter and disappear, and the changes are gradual enough that intermediate forms turn up in between — feathered dinosaurs sitting between reptiles and birds, four-legged whale ancestors with reduced hind limbs. The record is incomplete, because fossilisation is rare and many organisms leave nothing. But incompleteness is not the same as showing nothing, and the pattern through the layers is consistent everywhere it can be checked.

questions.stem: Why do bacteria evolve resistance quickly?
options: They live only in hospitals
They have no DNA to mutate
They reproduce very rapidly
They choose to change their DNA
questions.explanation: A new bacterial generation can appear in minutes, so useful mutations spread fast. Nothing is being chosen — the variation arises randomly and the antibiotic does the selecting.
questions.teaching:
Evolution needs generations, and generation time is what decides how fast it can run. Humans take twenty-odd years per generation. Some bacteria manage one in twenty minutes.

That is the main reason resistance appears so fast, and it is worth being careful about the mechanism. Nothing is choosing to change. Random variation means a few individuals in any large population already survive a given antibiotic; when the drug is used, those few are the ones left to reproduce, and the resistant version spreads. Finishing a prescribed course matters for exactly this reason — stopping early leaves behind the least susceptible survivors.

questions.stem: What is speciation?
options: The migration of a species
The forming of a new species
The extinction of a species
The naming of a species
questions.explanation: Speciation is one population splitting into two that can no longer interbreed, usually after long isolation. Naming a species is taxonomy, a human activity rather than a biological one.
questions.teaching:
A species is usually defined by breeding: its members can produce offspring that can themselves go on to breed. That definition is the key to this whole idea.

Now picture one population split in two — a mountain range rises, a river changes course, a handful of individuals reach an island. The two halves stop exchanging genes. Alterations to DNA accumulate separately in each, and the pressures acting on them differ. Given enough time the two drift so far apart that even if they met again they could no longer produce fertile young. At that point one population has become two. Note that it is the breeding barrier that marks the change, not merely looking different — dog breeds look wildly different and remain one species.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how the information in a gene becomes a protein?
options: DNA is translated into mRNA, which is transcribed into a chain of amino acids
DNA travels to the ribosome and is read directly into amino acids
mRNA is transcribed into DNA, which the ribosome reads as amino acids
DNA is transcribed into mRNA, which is translated into a chain of amino acids
questions.explanation: Transcription happens first, in the nucleus, and produces an mRNA copy of the gene. Translation happens second, at the ribosome, where the mRNA is read three bases at a time and the matching amino acids are joined into a chain. The names are worth keeping straight: translation is the step that changes language, from bases into amino acids.

questions.stem: A gene has the DNA sequence TAC GGA. What is the corresponding mRNA sequence?
options: AUG CCU
ATG CCT
AUG GGA
UAC GGA
questions.explanation: mRNA is built by matching complementary bases to the DNA template, so T pairs with A, A pairs with U, C pairs with G and G pairs with C. Applying that to TAC GGA gives AUG CCU. The key detail is that RNA uses uracil wherever DNA would use thymine, so no T ever appears in an mRNA answer.

questions.stem: What is a codon?
options: The full length of DNA that makes up one gene and its protein
The folded protein produced at the end of translation at a ribosome
A sequence of three mRNA bases that specifies one amino acid
A single mRNA base that specifies one amino acid in the chain
questions.explanation: The ribosome reads mRNA in groups of three, and each triplet is a codon that names one amino acid or signals a stop. Three bases give 64 possible combinations for 20 amino acids, which is why several codons share an amino acid. That spare capacity is the reason some mutations have no effect at all.

questions.stem: A single base substitution changes a codon from GAA to GAG, and both codons specify the amino acid glutamic acid. What type of mutation is this?
options: A silent mutation
A missense mutation
A nonsense mutation
A frameshift mutation
questions.explanation: The DNA changed but the protein did not, because both codons code for the same amino acid, and that is what silent means. A missense mutation would put a different amino acid in the chain and a nonsense mutation would insert a stop signal. Silent mutations are common precisely because the genetic code has more codons than amino acids.

questions.stem: A point mutation changes a codon so that it now reads as a stop codon partway through a gene. What type of mutation is this, and what is the likely effect?
options: A frameshift mutation, changing every amino acid after the point of change
A missense mutation, changing one amino acid in the chain
A nonsense mutation, producing a shortened and usually non-functional protein
A silent mutation, producing an identical protein
questions.explanation: A stop codon ends translation, so the amino acid chain is cut short and the protein is truncated. A protein that is missing part of its length almost never folds into the shape its job requires, so it is usually non-functional. A frameshift would require a base to be inserted or deleted rather than substituted.

questions.stem: Why is the insertion of a single base into a gene usually more damaging than the substitution of a single base?
options: An insertion always creates a stop codon at the point of insertion, ending translation
An insertion physically breaks the DNA molecule into two separate fragments
A substitution can never change which amino acid the codon specifies
An insertion shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is read wrongly
questions.explanation: The ribosome reads mRNA in fixed groups of three from a set starting point, so adding a base pushes every subsequent base into a different triplet. That makes the entire rest of the protein wrong, where a substitution can alter at most one amino acid. This is why a frameshift is defined by an insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a mutagen?
options: Sexual reproduction
Natural selection
Genetic drift
Ultraviolet radiation
questions.explanation: A mutagen is an agent that increases the rate at which mutations occur, and ultraviolet radiation does exactly that by damaging DNA directly. Sexual reproduction creates new combinations of existing alleles rather than new alleles, and natural selection acts on variation after it exists rather than causing it.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a skin cell of an adult. Why will this mutation not be passed to that person offspring?
options: Mutations can only occur in gametes
Only mutations in gametes are inherited
Skin cells repair every mutation before dividing
Mutations in body cells are always silent
questions.explanation: Offspring inherit DNA through egg and sperm cells, so only a mutation present in a gamete can be passed on. A mutation in a body cell can affect the person who carries it, which is how many cancers begin, but it never reaches the next generation. Distinguishing body cells from gametes is what this question is testing.

questions.stem: Two animals mate and produce offspring that are healthy but completely sterile. What does this tell you about the two parents?
options: They must be from the same population
They belong to different species
They belong to the same species
They are genetically identical
questions.explanation: The definition of a species requires that members interbreed to produce offspring that are themselves fertile. Offspring that cannot reproduce mean the two parents are separate species, which is exactly the horse and donkey case that produces a sterile mule. The word fertile in the definition carries the whole weight here.

questions.stem: A camel can tolerate a rise in its body temperature during the day, which reduces the water it loses through sweating. What type of adaptation is this?
options: Behavioural
Environmental
Physiological
Structural
questions.explanation: A physiological adaptation is an internal process or chemistry rather than a body part or an action, and temperature tolerance is a matter of how the body regulates itself. A structural adaptation would be a physical feature such as a hump or thick eyelashes, and a behavioural one would be something the camel does, such as resting in shade during the hottest hours.

questions.stem: Biodiversity is measured at three levels. Which set correctly names them?
options: Species diversity, family diversity and kingdom diversity
Genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity
Individual diversity, population diversity and species diversity
Genetic diversity, population diversity and habitat diversity
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is assessed as the variety of alleles within a species, the variety of species within an ecosystem, and the variety of ecosystems across a region. Counting species alone misses the genetic level, which matters because a large population with very little genetic variation has nothing for selection to act on if conditions change.

questions.stem: Which of these is a selection pressure acting on a population of rabbits?
options: An increase in the number of foxes hunting in the area
A random mutation arising in one rabbit
The reshuffling of alleles during reproduction
An increase in the number of alleles in the gene pool
questions.explanation: A selection pressure is a factor in the environment that affects which individuals survive and reproduce, and more predators is a clear example of a biotic one. Mutation and recombination are sources of variation rather than pressures acting on it. Keeping the source of variation separate from the pressure that selects among it is the central distinction in this topic.

questions.stem: Using the VEARC structure, which step must come first in an explanation of natural selection, and why?
options: Advantage, because the fittest individuals decide which variations will arise
Reproduction, because offspring must be produced before any selection can occur
Variation, because selection can only act on differences that already exist
Environmental pressure, because the environment creates the variation that is needed
questions.explanation: Variation has to be established first, because the whole mechanism depends on the population already containing inherited differences for the environment to select among. Starting with the pressure implies the environment produced the variation to order, which is the Lamarckian error the structure is designed to prevent. Answers that omit the variation step routinely lose the first mark.

questions.stem: In the VBSIS structure for speciation, what does the isolation step specifically require?
options: That gene flow between the two groups stops
That the two groups face identical selection pressures
That one group becomes extinct
That mutations stop occurring in both groups
questions.explanation: Isolation means no alleles pass between the separated groups, so the two gene pools change independently of each other. If migration and interbreeding continued, gene flow would keep mixing the populations and prevent them diverging far enough to become separate species. Different selection pressures on the two sides is a separate step, and both are needed.

questions.stem: What is gene flow?
options: The passing of alleles from parents to offspring within a single family line
The rate at which new mutations appear and spread through a population
The movement of mRNA out of the nucleus and towards the waiting ribosome
The movement of alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding
questions.explanation: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles from one population into another when individuals move and breed there, and it is what normally keeps populations of a species genetically united. Stopping gene flow is the requirement that lets two populations diverge, which is why a geographical barrier so often leads to speciation.

questions.stem: A bird wing and an insect wing both allow flight but developed independently in unrelated lineages. What term describes structures like these, and what do they demonstrate?
options: Homologous structures, demonstrating convergent evolution
Analogous structures, demonstrating convergent evolution
Homologous structures, demonstrating divergent evolution
Analogous structures, demonstrating divergent evolution
questions.explanation: Analogous structures share a function but not an ancestry, and they arise when unrelated lineages meet similar problems and arrive at similar solutions, which is convergent evolution. Homologous structures are the opposite case: a shared underlying anatomy such as the limb bones of a human arm, a whale flipper and a bat wing, adapted to different uses through divergent evolution.

questions.stem: How does comparative embryology provide evidence for evolution?
options: Embryos develop the same organs in a different order in each species
Embryonic development repeats the entire evolutionary history of the species
Vertebrate embryos pass through similar early stages, suggesting shared ancestry
Embryos of all species are identical until birth
questions.explanation: Early vertebrate embryos share features, including some the adult never keeps, and the most reasonable explanation is a developmental programme inherited from a common ancestor. The similarity is at early stages only, not throughout, and the stronger claim that development replays evolutionary history is an old idea that the evidence does not support.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, how do you determine which two species are most closely related?
options: By identifying which species appears furthest to the right
By finding which pair shares the most recent common ancestor
By seeing which pair is drawn closest together along the top
By measuring which pair has the shortest branches
questions.explanation: Relatedness is read by tracing each species back to the branch point they share, and the more recent that shared node the closer the relationship. Position along the top of the diagram carries no meaning, because any branch can be rotated without changing the relationships shown. Every species at the tips is equally modern.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a scientific theory and a hypothesis?
options: A theory is an untested guess about a process, a hypothesis is a statement already proven to be true
A theory applies only to living things, while a hypothesis applies only to physical and chemical processes
A theory has been proved beyond any possible doubt, while a hypothesis has not yet been tested at all
A theory is an explanation supported by a large body of evidence, a hypothesis is a testable prediction
questions.explanation: In science a theory is an explanatory framework that has survived extensive testing and is supported by evidence from many independent directions, which is why evolution is called one. A hypothesis is a specific testable statement, often the starting point of an investigation. The everyday use of theory to mean a hunch is what makes this distinction worth stating carefully.

questions.stem: A farmer breeds only the highest milk-yielding cows for many generations. Yield rises, but the herd becomes more prone to a particular inherited disease. Why?
options: Selecting hard for one trait narrows the gene pool, so harmful alleles become more common
Selective breeding causes new harmful mutations to appear in the animals that are chosen
Producing a high milk yield directly causes the inherited disease to develop in the animal
Cows bred for one trait lose the ability to pass beneficial alleles to their own offspring
questions.explanation: Breeding repeatedly from a small number of favoured animals reduces the genetic variation in the herd, so alleles that happen to travel with the desired trait, including harmful ones, rise in frequency. The process does not create new mutations, it concentrates existing ones. The same narrowing is why a genetically uniform crop can be destroyed by a single disease.
